subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBER'S BUSINESS-BILLS   FOOD AND DRUGS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 will be speaking on Bill C-289, an Act to amend the Food and Drugs Act, as tabled by the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps).
Bill C-289 addresses the problems of persons who, in a restaurant, unknowingly ingest food containing ingredients to which they are allergic. The Bill tabled in the House would compel each restaurant to make available for public consultation a list, in English or in French, of all the ingredients in any food sold by it.
The Bill would also compel each branch restaurant to afix on the packaging of any packaged foods sold by it a list, in English and in French, of the ingredients in such food.
The problem which Bill C-289 was introduced to solve is really quite acute in Canada. There are many persons who suffer from allergic reactions to various foods, food products or ingredients. There have even been some deaths caused by severe allergic reactions.
The Hon. Member for Hamilton East has pointed the finger at a considerable problem, and I want to thank her for raising the issue here in the House.
However, the motion of allergic reactions and how they are related to the foods we eat and our daily habits is in most cases ill-defined. In children, we see specific reactions to certain foods, and it is possible to prove that these reactions are due to allergies. Most adults are well aware that certain foods or beverages will cause digestive discomfort or allergic reactions, and that although the discomfort or reaction may not be serious, it is nevertheless unpleasant.
The impact of the substances in question tends to be worse when people are tense, nervous, tired or ill than when they are healthy and relaxed. Not enough is known as yet about the
actual mechanisms of such reactions, and they may depend far more on the characteristics of the person who consumed the allergy-causing product than on the product itself.
Consumers may suffer discomfort as a result of allergic reactions to substances used in the preparation of food, and this is even more likely to happen when they eat at a restaurant or eat food purchased from caterers.
By exercising a reasonable amount of care when shopping and cooking, a person can be reasonably sure of controlling the substances he eats in his own home. Thus, the individual who suffers from allergies will not be exposed to substances that may cause discomfort as long as he eats at home.
However, as soon as he goes to a restaurant or eats food purchased from a caterer, that control no longer exists. Anyone who eats food prepared outside the home has to assume the food does not contain any ingredients to which he could be allergic.
Madam Speaker, in the public mind, allergies may be related to the substances used in additives or preservatives, but that is not necessarily the case. For instance, allergies to basic foods such as nuts, seafood and dairy products are quite common. A person might order a meal in a French restaurant without knowing that a particular dish is prepared with a cream sauce, or in an oriental restaurant without being aware that the meal includes a peanut sauce. Some people are allergic to certain types of oil or certain kinds of flour.
Furthermore, today's foods are prepared in a very complex way or in recipes with many ingredients. Often, many additives and preservatives are used, which may produce allergic reactions in some individuals.
We know that various substances may produce different reactions in some people. There is no question here of casting doubt on some foods or wondering whether some restaurants use unsafe ingredients. Agriculture Canada and Health and Welfare Canada have published strict regulations regarding food safety and freshness and the nature of additives.
Additives that present a complex risk are banned or subject to very strict control, like sulphites, for example, on which the Government recently imposed strict control after it was shown that they caused too many allergic reactions. Health and Welfare Canada now prohibits their use on all fruit and vegetables sold or served fresh, except grapes.
When people who are subject to allergies consume certain substances, a whole series of physiological effects that may produce reactions occurs and therein lies the problem. This is a matter of information in general and health affecting all consumers. We must ask ourselves how to inform those subject to allergic reactions, who therefore cannot take the chance of consuming food made outside the home.
July 7, 1988

Bill C-289, although incomplete and imperfect, allows us to take a step forward by offering a possible solution. I am sure that officials at Health and Welfare Canada and Consumer and Corporate Affairs will carefully study it in detail, while continuing to protect the health and safety of Canadian consumers. I am also sure, Madam Speaker, that they will continue to discover ways to protect persons suffering from food allergies.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBER'S BUSINESS-BILLS   FOOD AND DRUGS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Hamilton-East (Ms. Copps) has tabled Bill C-289, an Act to amend the Food and Drugs Act. This Bill would compel restaurants to make available for public consultation a list in English and in French, of all the ingredients in any foods sold by them. This Bill, madam Speaker, would also compel caterers to affix on the packaging of any packaged food they sell, in French and in English, a list of all the ingredients they use.
The purpose of Bill C-289 is to protect consumers who may have allergic reactions to various foods or to the ingredients in such food. The Bill, madam Speaker, proposes to solve this problem by forcing restaurants to provide a list of the ingredients they use.
Madam Speaker, the problem is the same for consumers who buy food in food stores. Consumers may also in that case have allergic reactions and that must be taken into consideration. In so far as food purchased in food stores is concerned, the problem is partially resolved by the listing of ingredients as required by food and drug regulations.
However, the requirement to list ingredients on prepackaged foods was not conceived with allergic persons in mind, but to give consumers a list, in decreasing order, of the various substances contained in the foods they purchase.
Madam Speaker, it is the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs that has the responsibility of managing the labelling, packaging, and marketing of foods, pursuant to the Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act and regulations and the Food and Drugs Act. The Health Protection Branch of the Department of Health and Welfare advises the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs on the labelling and marketing of products that have any bearing on health.
Madam Speaker, various information is required on the labels of pre-packaged foods, such as the following.
1)	The common name of the food;
2)	The net quantity of the contents;
3)	The name and address of the person or company that produced the food;
4)	The list of ingredients;
5)	The shelf life of the food and preservation instructions.
All this information must be provided, in French and in English. The only exceptions are the name and address of the manufacturer which may be printed in either of the official languages of this country. And I refer you to Bill C-72.
Food and Drugs Act
Madam Speaker, as we are now debating Bill C-289, it is important to mention that it is the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs that was entrusted with the responsibility for these labelling requirements.
That is understandable as these measures were adopted to protect the consumer. The consumer must know what he is buying. He must be aware of the quality of the product and be sure it is not being sold on the basis of misleading advertising.
Madam Speaker, this is a very important point, and 1 want to make it clear that our present labelling requirements which have been in effect since the early seventies and are quite strict and effective, are above all aimed at protecting the consumer. However, while Bill C-289 is also aimed at protecting the consumer's health, its purpose is to protect the consumer against the possibility of allergic reactions to allergens in food consumed in restaurants. As I said before, neither the Food and Drugs Act nor the regulations on labelling were designed to indentify allergens.
However, Madam Speaker, the public is demanding specific information on ingredients and components of the food offered in restaurants and by suppliers.
Madam Speaker, Canadians are eating more and more meals outside the home. Every year, the percentage of our income spent on restaurant meals and on food purchased outside the home is increasing considerably, and the number and popularity of fast food restaurants is increasing as well.
Furthermore, Madam Speaker, a number of Canadians suffering from allergies is important. Canadians are concerned about their health and, according to public opinion polls, they are aware of allergy problems. The use of additives, preservatives and colouring agents is often challenged, especially if they contain allergens. That is why food processors often indicate on their labels the fact that their products do not contain such substances.
There are also certain whole foods that may cause allergies without containing additives or preservatives. We know that some people are allergic to nuts, fish, the gluten found in corn and wheat and to dairy products.
In the last few decades, Madam Speaker, food technology has made tremendous progress. Many foods and food products are subject to complex processes or combine a large number of ingredients. All this increases the complexity of our food and also increases our chances of having an allergy.
For all these reasons, Madam Speaker, Canadians who are at risk should be offered a margin of safety when they go out to a restaurant, especially since this is becoming an increasingly common social custom.
In concluding, I would say that Bill C-289 is a step forward. However, we must not forget that identifying ingredients is only one of the solutions to the problem we are facing today. This legislation will certainly be a first step, but there are other questions that remain to be answered.

July 7, 1988
Food and Drugs Act
For instance, publishing exhaustive lists would preclude any substitution, and so a chef would no longer be free to be creative. If there is a shortage of a particular ingredient, another ingredient cannot be substituted. Chefs would no longer be free to improvise and follow their inspiration. Restaurants that offer daily specials, and these are usually the smaller establishments, would have trouble meeting these requirements.
Bill C-289 is a good start, Madam Speaker. Many Canadians suffer from allergies, and we must consider the problems they may face when they go out to a restaurant. Bill C-289 would seem to suggest a number of solutions, but there is room for improvement. A start has been made, but what we need now is further debate and discussion that will lead to satisfactory solutions.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBER'S BUSINESS-BILLS   FOOD AND DRUGS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to speak to Bill C-289 which has focused the attention of the House on the problems faced by many Canadians who suffer from various food allergies. This Bill would require the mandatory listing of the ingredients used in restaurant foods.
I want to compliment my colleague for introducing this Bill. It is important to make the Canadian public more aware of the problem. Indeed, I have spoken to a number of my constituents who have food allergies and they say that it is very necessary for restaurants to list food ingredients. I believe the House of Commons and the Government can find a solution to this problem.
Food allergies constitute a real problem for a significant number of Canadians. According to a recent report on Global News, 25,000 Canadians are at risk every day because of their food allergies. Other reports have stated that in Canada over the past two years at least 24 people have died from allergic reactions to food after having eaten in restaurants. This is a very frightening statistic to anyone with a dangerous food allergy.
There has been a recent precedent set in the area of food allergy and adverse reaction. In the early 1980s, sulphites, a group of substances that had been widely used as preservatives for years, received a good deal of public attention as the possible cause of a number of allergic reactions suffered by people eating in restaurants. In some cases the adverse reactions were severe enough to require medical attention and even hospitalization.
The health protection branch of Health and Welfare Canada has consulted with many expert sources on this issue. Meetings and consultations were held with groups such as The Allergy Information Association, the Canadian Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology, the medical community, regulatory agencies from other countries, and the Canadian Restaurant and Food Services Association, which has resulted in a clearer picture of the problem.
We have learned that the use of sulphites on fresh fruits and vegetables in salad bars, for example, was the most common source of problems. Restaurants like to use sulphites to keep the salad ingredients looking fresh.
However, in further meetings with the Canadian Restaurant and Food Services Association, that organization took voluntary steps to discourage the use of sulphites by its members. In addition to that voluntary initiative, the health protection branch went further. It felt it prudent to enact regulations prohibiting the use of sulphites.
It also carried out a consumer education program on the use of sulphites through the use of fact sheets and brochures. Based on all the available information, these have been effective and the problem with sulphites has been minimized.
I have spoken about sulphites at some length because there is at least a rough parallel between the way that issue was handled and the way a solution to the problem of allergic reactions to restaurant food is emerging. As I said, a number of unfortunate and even tragic incidents have occurred, and the media has reported on this issue.
Members know that we are now in a period of discussion and consultation, not the least caused by the introduction of this Bill. The Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare has held hearings on the topic. Officials of both Health and Welfare Canada and the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs are actively seeking the best possible solution to the problem. Extensive discussions are being held with the allergy association, the medical community, and the Canadian Restaurant and Food Services Association.
In a very encouraging development, the private sector is again addressing itself to resolving a very serious problem. The Canadian Restaurant and Food Services Association is strongly encouraging a voluntary program among its 6,800 member companies. In fact, according to a recent report by Canadian Press, industry spokesmen have said that restaurant menus should warn consumers of ingredients that could lead to allergic reactions before they order a meal. The Vice-President of the Restaurant and Food Service Association was also quoted as saying that a system of warning charts could be introduced in quick service chains because they have highly centralized control over ingredients.
The consistency of the menus in chain restaurants, combined with the limited choices available, make the charts a manageable idea. According to the same Canadian Press report, the association has talked to 24 national quick service chains, and 22 of them have agreed to take part in the allergy chart idea.
This is good news. It shows that the food services industry is well aware of the problem and is more than willing to take steps to resolve it. It further shows that the idea of an ingredients list, if it can be fine-tuned and made manageable and practical, is indeed a good one.
July 7, 1988

However, there are some questions yet to be answered regarding ingredients list. What about the ingredients that went into the butter that is in the cake which is in the final product? Just how comprehensively would disclosure requirements be applied to sellers of food? Would they apply to owners of chip wagons and vendors of hotdogs at the Sparks Street Mall and at our ballparks?
The breadth and scope of the food service industry presents a very real challenge in this area. It is so diverse and widespread that any new programs must take these qualities into consideration.
Bill C-289 is serving a very useful purpose in getting the public to think seriously about the issue of food allergies and restaurant food. However, it leaves these and many other questions unanswered. It may very well be that the listing of restaurant food ingredients is the best way to tackle the issue. Indeed, present thinking by both industry and all of us concerned about allergies seems to be along these lines.
In the event that ingredients lists are the way to go, every effort must be made to see to it that the listing system that is adopted is the best possible one that can be put in place. In this area it does seem certain that Bill C-289 can be significantly improved.
It is essential that consumers get the information they need to protect themselves in the market-place and to make intelligent choices. This applies as much to allergy sufferers who dine in restaurants as it does to anyone else.
The Government is determined to bring about an effective solution to the issue. If that solution is to centre upon ingredients disclosure lists, the House can be assured that listing requirements will be applied in a manner that is effective, fair, and as cost-efficient as possible. I say this because some of the attraction in dining out, particularly at fast food or quick service outlets, is that prices are reasonable and obviously affordable to a great number of Canadians. We want to make sure that it stays that way.
We must adopt a system that affords the best possible protection to the Canadian consumer and allows greater freedom and safety for the sufferer of food allergies.
[ Translation]

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBER'S BUSINESS-BILLS   FOOD AND DRUGS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I shall speak on Bill C-289, an Act to amend the Food and Drugs Act, tabled by the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps).
Bill C-289 is concerned with the problems of those who, in a restaurant, unknowingly eat food containing ingredients to which they are allergic. The Bill tabled in the House would require every restaurant to make available to the public a list in French and English of all the ingredients used in the food sold.
Food and Drugs Act
The Bill would also require every branch of a restaurant and every restaurant chain to indicate on all packaging a list in French and English of the ingredients used in the food.
The problem that Bill C-289 seeks to deal with is really acute in Canada. Many people suffer allergic reactions to various foods, food products or ingredients. People have even died from severe allergic reactions. The Hon. Member for Hamilton East has put her finger on a considerable problem and she must be thanked for bringing it to the House of Commons.
The concept of allergic reaction itself, and its relationship to diet and daily habits, are unfortunately undefined in most circumstances. Children have particular reactions to some foods and it is possible to show that these reactions are due to allergies. Almost all adults know very well that some foods or drinks will disturb their digestion or cause allergic reactions, which, although not serious, are nevertheless unpleasant.
The troublesome substances cause even more problems when people are tense, frightened, tired or sick than when they are well and relaxed. How such reactions occur is still little known and may have much more to do with the characteristics of the individual who ate the product that caused the allergy than with the characteristics of the product itself.
Consumers may suffer from allergic reactions to substances used in food preparation and this is more likely to occur when they eat in a restaurant or eat food supplied by a caterer.
By being careful when shopping and cooking, someone can be reasonably sure of controlling the substances eaten at home. Thus, an allergic individual keeps away from troublesome substances when eating at home. But when he eats in a restaurant or eats food purchased from a caterer, the person cannot monitor things as closely. Thus, a person who eats food prepared outside his home must take it for granted that such food does not contain any ingredient to which he might be allergic.
Madam Speaker, public opinion has it that allergies may be related to substances used in additives or preservatives. But that is not necessarily the case. For instance, many people are allergic to such staple foods as nuts, seafood, and dairy products. One might easily order a meal in a French restaurant without knowing that a given dish comes with a cream sauce, or in an oriental restaurant without knowing that a meal will be served with a peanut sauce. Some persons will have allergic reactions to certain oils or to certain types of flour.
Furthermore, it must be said that today's foods undergo complex preparation or are made from recipes containing a multitude of ingredients. Often, many additives and preservatives are used, ingredients which may provoke allergic reactions in some people.

July 7, 1988
Food and Drugs Act
We know that different substances can produce different reactions in some people. Our purpose here is not to call into question the safety of certain foods nor to ask whether some restaurants are using dangerous ingredients. Agriculture Canada and Health and Welfare Canada have published strict regulations on food safety, its freshness and the nature of additives used.
When additives do present a complex risk, they are banned or subjected to very strict controls, as was the case for sulfites, on which the Government recently imposed strict controls, after it was shown that these substances were causing too many allergic reactions.
So, Health and Welfare Canada now prohibits the use of such substances on any produce sold or served fresh, excepting grapes.
When certain substances are consumed by individuals subject to allergies they trigger a whole series of physiological sequences that may result in reactions, and there lies the problem. This is a comprehensive disclosure issue, a health issue that involves all consumers. We must ask ourselves how we can inform people who may be subject to allergic reactions, but who for that reason cannot consume food that is prepared outside their homes.
Bill C-289 gives us an opportunity to make a step forward by proposing a possible solution, albeit incomplete and imperfect.
I am convinced that officials of Health and Welfare Canada and Consumer and Corporate Affairs Canada will review the details in a careful way, while Continuing to ensure the health and safety of Canadian consumers.
Madam Speaker, I am also convinced they will go on finding ways to ensure the protection of people with food allergies.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBER'S BUSINESS-BILLS   FOOD AND DRUGS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Bill C-289 comes as a commendable effort to limit a serious consumer problem. It is aimed at providing the information they need to individuals who may suffer from allergic reactions to foods they eat in restaurants.
The current packaging and labelling Act and regulations work toward that goal by requiring disclosure of information on foods that are bought in food stores. Under that Act, most foods sold in food stores must be labelled in both official languages. That requirement covers both foreign and domestic products.
Canadian consumers are entitled to complete information in both official languages on the food they buy. As consumers, they must have an opportunity to make informed choices, and to that end they are entitled to get in the language with which they are more familiar information that will guide their choices.
The Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act requires certain compulsory information, and the regulations prescribe that information be supplied in both French and English.
Current requirements cover the common name of the food, the net weight of the product, the name and address of the relevant firm, the list of ingredients and directions as to the shelf life and preservation of the product.
Since its enactment in 1972, that Act has been working well: it is consistent, and both producers and entrepreneurs know it well. Suppliers know what is expected from them, and they provide on the labels bilingual information meeting the requirements.
With respect to the list of ingredients, most prepackaged food must have one showing either the decreasing order of ingredients or the percentage of their use. There are exceptions of course, and here are some of them:
-Repackaged products from bulk retail production;
-Prepackaged individual portions served with meals and snacks in restaurants;
-Individual portions prepared by a supplier and sold in vending machines or mobile canteens;
-Standard alcoholic beverages;
-Vinegar.
None of the standards specified in the Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act applies to food sold in restaurants or other similar establishments. In such places, people suffering from allergies might unknowingly run the risk of eating food or substances to which they are allergic. In some cases the ensuing allergic reaction is serious and, now and then, it may even be fatal.
Bill C-289 is a commendable effort aimed at eliminating such situations and providing consumers with the information to which they are entitled with respect to foods served in restaurants. It is a step in the right direction, but the motion of the Hon. Member is very brief. The question has a number of aspects with which the motion does not deal, and it can be improved in many ways.
For instance, the restaurant business has to be a very flexible undertaking. Various ingredients may be available to the chef today but not tomorrow. Many restaurants change menus regularly-every day, in some cases-to offer a better choice to their patrons and take advantage of what is available on the market. It would be next to impossible for a restaurant-or even an establishment which has printing facilities- to provide clients with the full list of ingredients used to prepare daily menus.
Think of the many ingredients used to prepare a French sauce, for instance, or any other food dish. Menus would be ridiculously bulky and practically illegible. Ethnic restaurants would have to deal with the added problem of translating the names of exotic ingredients without being in a position to guarantee that an allergy-prone customer would be protected against unknown ingredients. Such an excess of information might cause a real problem.
July 7, 1988

Moreover, customers suffering from food allergies might get a false sense of security with such a list of ingredients. The risk of error remains high. One single lapse in concentration and an additional ingredient in a recipe could have unfortunate results. Not even a minimal substitution or change would be allowed. In view of the very nature of restaurants, this is hardly a reasonable attempt.
Certain practical difficulties associated with the production and labelling of foods should be taken into account.
Madam Speaker, Bill C-289 deals with a problem which I feel is real and should be dealt with. I wonder, however, if this Bill is really the best possible way to protect Canadians suffering from food allergies.
For instance, some believe that we could require restaurant owners to provide upon request to consumers suffering from food allergies a verbal list of all their ingredients.
This would have the benefit of immediate effectiveness while relieving the restaurant owner of the obligation and costs of a printed menu. Good restaurants-I do not mean the most expensive ones-willingly provide such information. Fast food operators could have a list of ingredients which could be distributed upon request.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if such suggestions are likely to help solve the problem. But we must of necessity examine all proposals which could help us protect Canadians suffering from food allergies.
Through its committee responsible for warning labels on food and drug packaging, the House of Commons addressed this issue once before. On the other hand, the officials at Consumer and Corporate Affairs Canada and Health and Welfare Canada continue to look for all possible ways to help Canadians suffering from allergies. There is no doubt that Bill C-289 will greatly help us solve this problem.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBER'S BUSINESS-BILLS   FOOD AND DRUGS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going to speak to this Bill very briefly as one who has had personal experience with an allergic reaction which necessitated my going to the hospital on three occasions, twice here in the national capital area, in fact to the Riverside Hospital, and once in Nairobi, Africa, where I took a severe allergic reaction to some foods that 1 had eaten. One instance, in fact, caused me to go into a very difficult breathing period when I thought I was going to pass out and die. I can relate very closely to this Bill from a personal point of view.
The Bill is entitled Bill C-289, an Act to amend the Food and Drugs Act. This Bill is designed to help Canadians with food allergies when they eat out at restaurants or places that supply fast foods. As you know, Sir, there are many within our country. We had a very unfortunate incident recently in which a young lady in the National Capital Region died from an
Food and Drugs Act
allergic reaction to some nuts that she ate which she did not realize were in the food she had consumed.
The particular Bill here would have a dual effect. First, it would require every restaurant to make available for the public consultation, a list in English and French, of all the ingredients in any foods sold by it. The Bill would also compel each branch restaurant of a restaurant chain to affix on the packaging of any foods sold by it a list in English and in French of the ingredients in such food.
Many thousands of Canadians suffer from food allergies. They are described in some contexts as a nuisance. I guess I can describe my own as a nuisance because it did not persist for very long. However, for some Canadians they can be much greater than a nuisance, they can be deadly.
The CBC reported quite recently that in the last two years upward of 24 persons have died in Canada from severe allergies to foods. As things now stand, while most packaged foods sold in food stores have labelling requirements for ingredients and quantities, there are as yet no mandatory labelling requirements for restaurant food. Instead, individuals with food allergies have to ask the appropriate questions as to whether the ingredients in a restaurant food will trigger an allergic reaction. In other words, it is incumbent upon the person who goes to a restaurant to eat to ask those questions.
Therefore this Bill is performing a very valuable service in so far as it is causing a much greater debate on the subject, and in that it is raising the question of whether or not the present system is adequate. Certainly, Canadian consumers deserve the best possible protection, whether they buy food in a supermarket for preparation and consumption at home or whether they go out and eat in a restaurant, be that restaurant a very humble one or a very luxurious one.
The Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare has heard testimony recently on this issue from the Canadian Food and Restaurant Association and, in particular, Mr. Bill Dover, who is the President of Red Lobster of Canada which, in principle, is supporting the directions of this Bill. I hope that in due course the House will do the same thing.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not surprising to find in Bill C-124, respecting the amendments to the Canada Labour Code, that we have a number of technical amendments at this time. It is amazing that the amendments are in the name of a Member who is not a member of the legislative committee. Usually members of the legislative committee make amendments. It is not unusual that we have this number of amendments, because committee study on Bill C-124 was a rush job. Government Members would not allow the committee to call any witnesses other than the Minister and his staff, nor would they allow a second meeting of the committee.
Let me refresh Hon. Members' memories. The committee met on May 9, 1988 at 3.38 p.m. The Minister and one of his officials appeared with him. I asked permission to contact members of the unions involved and the only employer involved in the case. The request was denied by members of the committee. I asked that there be a second meeting so that we could study the legislation. Again, government Members refused.
As a result of the process all the clauses of the Bill were passed by 5.07 p.m. The Bill was studied in committee for only one and a half hours. The Minister and his official spoke. We had a procedural squabble over the desire to have witnesses who would know what this legislation would do to them.
I said that we would not stall the legislation, that what we wanted was the right to have witnesses "one week hence", and that I was able to guarantee the legislation would pass committee stage that day or the following one. Conservative members on that committee, I believe on instructions from the Department, refused to allow any witnesses whatever.
This piece of legislation was allowed through second reading on the basis of one afternoon's debate. This was not legislation that the Opposition was stalling. This was not legislation that was even being opposed by the opposition Parties. We recognized that as Members of Parliament we had an obligation to allow people who would be affected to make their presentations, to explain what they believed should be in the legislation, but the request was denied and I believe Parliament failed in its duty in doing so.
Today, two nionths after the Government refused to have a second meeting of this committee, the legislation was brought to the House. Obviously any time during those two months we could have heard from witnesses. This was not a matter of pressing and urgent necessity. This was an example of government arrogance, an example of the Government refusing to listen to those affected, an example of the Government assuming that it knew better than any of those who would be affected.
The Minister has admitted that one of the opposition motions is better than his own Department's. He has withdrawn his own amendment. We have other amendments that
are probably technically better than the Government's amendments. In addition, we have a number of what 1 would call controversial issues dealing with the work site which were never raised in the House of Commons. Motion No. 6 speaks to that.
Motion No. 3 was ruled out of order and speaks to a matter of controversy and concern to people in the workforce. As well, since this legislation was rushed through committee study, the Minister himself has received representations from one union, the Canadian Union of Public Employees whose members work at the plant. The union would like to see the committee looking at workplace safety being restructured so that it could include a representative of the union, but that will not happen.
I do not have much time to explain all these points because 1 am limited to speaking for only 10 minutes. However, I think what I have said sets the groundwork. This legislation is coming to the House flawed. The process that we went through was very objectionable. It denied us the advice of people who will be directly affected by the legislation. It prevents Parliament from resolving some of the difficulties of people who work in the mines at Cape Breton.
Some suggestions were made to the Minister, and he knows that. There is a conflict among the unions in Cape Breton, and the Minister also knows that. Had the committee had the opportunity in one afternoon to hear from a representative of each of the three unions involved, as well as from the management, perhaps we could have amended this Bill in a manner that would have met all concerns. I do not believe the issues were without any possibility of being resolved. Instead, the House of Commons committee refused to allow these problems to be resolved and, worse than that, the committee refused even to allow the participants any sort of a fair hearing.
This legislation affects only one employer. It affects only three groups of unionized workers. I do not believe the House of Commons was in such a rush that we could not have heard from them. I do not believe our agenda was so tight that we could not have heard from them. I find it very regrettable that Conservative Members refused to allow witnesses to appear. As a result the legislation will not meet the needs of all workers at that work site, particularly those of the Canadian Union of Public Employees.
The legislation we have is meant to prevent fires and explosions at the work site. We accept and support that, but for some reason the Minister and his officials have deemed it necessary to give the employer the right to search for drugs, alcohol, and other goods. If the purpose of the legislation is to prevent explosions and fires, then we should certainly allow for searches for those goods which would directly cause explosions and fires. Obviously smoking materials could do that and, therefore it would obviously be correct to search for those items. That is something to which the employees agreed as well.


July 7, 1988

I find it unusual that in this legislation we are granting an employer a right we do not grant any other employer who falls under the Canada Labour Code. I must ask the Minister why he is setting this precedent in this legislation. I believe that is why he has reserved his right to speak after me on this amendment. Why would he introduce this widespread power when the legislation is supposed to give an employer a very specific right to deal with a very specific problem?
I appreciate that you have given me some extra time, Madam Speaker, because of the complexity of the situation. While the Minister is on his feet, perhaps he could explain if this legislation granting this extraordinary right under the Canada Labour Code will set a precedent for other legislation that the Minister might be introducing.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank Hon. Members who, by unanimous consent, granted me the right and the privilege to speak after the movers of the motion had done so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to propose to the House today, on behalf of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse), a package of amendments to Bill C-75 dealing with an issue of deep concern to Nova Scotians, the protection of the Georges Bank fishery.
There is no dispute that the Georges Bank fishery is an important economic resource for Canada, the Province of Nova Scotia, and the people of southwestern Nova Scotia in particular.
The Government was fully aware of the importance of the Georges Bank fishery. It was also very much aware of the environmental sensitivity of the Bank and of the concerns being expressed by the Government of Nova Scotia and by the people of region over the potential impact that petroleum activity could have on the Bank. Therefore, discussions were held with the Energy Minister and the Premier of Nova Scotia and others on how best to satisfactorily resolve the impasse.
It was agreed, following these extensive discussions and consultations, that there should be a full and open public review of the environmental and socio-economic issues related to petroleum activities on the Georges Bank.
There had also been the concern expressed that such an environmental review conducted under the auspices of the Oil and Gas Management Board would not provide the objectivity this important issue deserved. As a result, it was agreed that the review would be conducted by an independent panel rather than the new Offshore Oil and Gas Management Board.

July 7, 1988

The Georges Bank is a unique fishery resource, and unique measures are required in the circumstances to balance the interests of all concerned. The moratorium and public review process will provide assurances to all Canadians that the Government understands the seriousness of environmental concerns and how these relate to other major considerations in our lives.
An agreement was reached with the Government of Nova Scotia on an amendment package for Georges Bank which contains the following key provisions. First, a moratorium is to be put in place on oil and gas activity on the Georges Bank until at least the year 2000.
Second, prior to the year 1996 an independent review panel will be constituted to hold public hearings on the environmental and social impacts of drilling on the Bank. The panel will report to the federal and provincial Ministers of Energy on or before July 1, 1999. The Ministers will then jointly decide whether the ban on petroleum activity should be extended beyond January 1, 2000.
These amendments will bring the federal accord legislation into line with that of the Province of Nova Scotia whose legislature passed the Georges Bank amendment package on May 25, 1988. The decisions embodied in the Georges Bank amendment package represent a credible solution to a very sensitive issue, one which is widely supported as being in the best public interest. I am pleased that the Governments of Canada and Nova Scotia, working together in a climate of cooperation, were able to resolve this issue.
I am today asking this House to join with others in supporting these measures by giving the amendments its stamp of approval.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I introduce, on behalf of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse), final reading on Bill C-75, an Act to implement the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Petroleum Resources Accord. The Bill before the House will implement the Canada-Nova Scotia Accord that was signed on August 26, 1986, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and by the Premier of Nova Scotia, John Buchanan. Lying at the heart of the legislation is a new shared management regime under which the province has an equal say in decisions. This will significantly improve on the arrangements contained in the 1982 agreement with Nova Scotia, pursuant to which the province had only an advisory role in a federally controlled system.
The legislation will create a new independent board to administer and regulate petroleum activities in the offshore on behalf of the two Governments. The board will have considerable autonomy on technical decisions but will be subject to the joint direction of the two Governments on any fundamental decisions.
The legislation will convert the $200 million offshore development fund created under the 1982 agreement into a grant. Above and beyond this, the Government of Canada will make available a new $25 million fund to Nova Scotia Resources Ventures Limited, to assist in participating in exploration and development drilling in the offshore area.
This legislation incorporates existing federal legislation, the Canada Petroleum Resources Act and the Oil and Gas Production Act, so that there will be consistency in the legal framework for oil and gas activity in all offshore areas of Canada. This is highly desirable, from both an industry and government perspective, in ensuring consistently safe and well understood practices to be applied in all coastal areas.
In conclusion, the legislation will assure the Government of Nova Scotia of its rightful place alongside the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador as an equal partner with the Government of Canada in the management of petroleum resources of the East Coast.
The legislation will set aside the question of which level of government has jurisdiction over the offshore resources in favour of a joint management regime under which these resources are managed together for the benefit of all Canadians and, particularly, those in Nova Scotia.
It will thus create a stable investment climate to encourage industry investment by eliminating the risk that jurisdictional disputes will delay important project decisions.
July 7, 1988

The Government of Nova Scotia has passed into law the provincial legislation implementing the Nova Scotia Accord. I would ask this House to join with Nova Scotia in sanctioning this important legislation, thereby taking Canada one more purposeful step forward in national reconciliation and full realization of the benefits that will flow from the accord.

Although this Bill was initiated with offshore petroleum resource management, it was made clearly evident by representatives of the Nova Scotia fishing industry that protection of the fishery was of equivalent importance to oil and gas resources and had to be given consideration within the framework of this Bill. I think that is rightly put forward.
I want to thank also at this point the representatives of the fishing industry who came before the committee and, particularly, the organization known as NORIG, for their very relevant and in-depth presentation and support given to all committee members.
According to the accord to which this Bill relates, which was originally signed on the August 26, 1986, one of its seven major objectives was as follows: "To achieve the early development of petroleum resources in the offshore area for the benefit of Canada as a whole and Nova Scotia in particular". This statement overlooked the fact that there is a traditional resource in Nova Scotia, and that is, the fishery.
To act for the benefit of Canada as a whole and Nova Scotia in particular, we have to give particular attention to the fishery. Georges Bank is the most prolific fishery grounds in the world. That is of tremendous importance to the Province of Nova Scotia. It is many times more prolific than any other fishing grounds in the world, and of course there are a great many good fishing grounds throughout the world.
Six thousand people in the Province of Nova Scotia depend on the fishing industry directly related to Georges Bank. If we did not heed the seriousness of drilling in Georges Bank then
Canada-Nova Scotia Accord
the quality of life in Nova Scotia could be set off balance as a result of petroleum exploration and development. As a result, we have this amendment, which places a 12-year moratorium on oil and gas exploration and development on the Canadian side of Georges Bank. We establish by this amendment as well a review panel which will report on the environmental and socio-economic impact of exploration and drilling activities in this specific area by January 1, 1996.
Bill C-75 acted as a catalyst to make the legislative committee in the House of Commons confront the needs of the region, ensure the best use of the offshore resources, including the fishery, and put in place a process which will provide an equal hearing to those with differing concerns on offshore resource management.
I think that sets up the framework that all Canadians would like to see. There are, of course, various interests that will not be satisfied by this, but I think that what has been put in place is fair, and certainly fair to the fishing industry of Nova Scotia.
The situation on the Georges Bank highlighted three factors which are relevant to making decisions about resource development and management; socio-economic concerns, scientific evidence, and the political objectives of the people.
This proposed legislation provides a viable process for federal-provincial co-operation on offshore petroleum resource management. As I mentioned in my speech during second reading, the process will have limited use as no resource development is currently taking place. The lack of a coherent energy policy by this Government has led to merely ad hoc initiatives which may or may not be in the long-term interests of Canadians. This is why we did not have these very important provisions in the original Bill.
Furthermore, the objective of the Government, "to protect, preserve and advance the attainment of national security of supply" of energy resources, will be superseded by the terms of the free trade agreement.
The development of offshore resources is more likely to be based on decisions by U.S. multinationals whose objective it is to supply U.S. markets rather than plan to meet the future needs of Canadians. 1 do not think that that is wrong. The energy multinationals have played a very important role in the development of oil and gas and energy needs of this country and they are to be congratulated and thanked by the Canadian public.
However, there is a limit. One cannot expect oil companies, multinational or otherwise, to act in the interests of the fishing industry of Nova Scotia. It just makes common sense that oil companies have their vested interests. Fishermen and the fishing industry have their vested interests. This is why it is paramount that the Governments of this country look at situations like this and come down on the side of the people, the best interests of the people and the region in which they live. This is being done with the amendments that have been brought forward here this evening in the House of Commons at report stage. I feel good about this Bill. It certainly has the support of my Party as amended.

July 7, 1988
Canada-Nova Scotia Accord
The fact that the Government has failed the people of Canada on two counts is demonstrated by the response of the Nova Scotian community to the idea of oil and gas drilling on Georges Bank. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources failed to develop a national energy strategy upon which regional initiatives would be based to ensure a security of supply.
In addition, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) and other members of the Government have not taken into consideration, or did not take into consideration initially, the needs of the fishing industry in Nova Scotia. It was really members of the fishing industry and the communities involved that brought to the attention of the Government the need for these amendments, both here and in the Province of Nova Scotia.
This is one of the finest examples we will see in Canada of people interested in a particular resource knowing that they could lose the very vital industry on which their incomes and their livelihoods have come to depend. They have reached out to the Government and made their presentation in a forceful and objective manner. They have succeeded in having the Government, all Members of the House of Commons, and all members of the Legislature of the Province of Nova Scotia, listen to their arguments and accept their validity.
To have shown a disregard and a lack of empathy for the needs of the people dependent on the Georges Bank fishery would have been a catastrophe. It would have been a very bad example to the rest of the country. It would have been devastating for the people of Nova Scotia. We now have these amendments which are the results of this positive process which was initiated by the people in southwest Nova Scotia.
In addition to serving the needs of Nova Scotians and Canadians, the amended legislation is playing a leadership role in gaining U.S. support to prohibit oil and gas drilling on its portion of the Georges Bank. In June, the United States House Appropriations Committee voted to extend the one-year moratorium on any sites less than 400 metres deep. Previously, this restriction was only on 60 metre sites. Thus, that committee has increased protection of the U.S. side of the Georges Bank to almost 7 million acres.
This is a direct result of the action taken by the Government of Canada and the Government of the Province of Nova Scotia to say that we are not going to be drilling on Georges Bank during the moratorium period of 12 years. Had we not listened to the fishing community in Nova Scotia and to the concerns of Nova Scotians in general, and had we allowed the possibility of drilling to occur on Georges Bank, then this would have set a precedent for the United States. It could very well have followed suit. Not only have we prevented the drilling on the
Canadian side of Georges Bank, we have also prevented drilling on the United States side of Georges Bank.
Some people may ask why we should worry about the United States side. Primarily, it is because the current in Georges Bank goes in a circular motion. Any spills or debris that is thrown into the bank comes around on to the Nova Scotia and the Canadian side. Any debris, any spillage, any pollution of any kind not only pollutes the side on which it occurs but it pollutes both sides of the border.
Canada is establishing an admirable precedent with this legislation. We have decided that the fishery as a resource takes precedence over petroleum resources until it is proven that no damage will be incurred to the Georges Bank or to the quality of life in Nova Scotia.
All the politicians in the Province of Nova Scotia and almost all of the politicians in the House of Commons-certainly all the members of my Party-have decided that we will not risk sacrificing the fishery in order to promote oil and gas development, particularly since this country does not have a comprehensive energy policy. We would be throwing darts in the dark if we were to allow drilling since we would not know what exactly would occur from any commencement of activity on the Georges Bank.
In this instance, the democratic process has worked. Nova Scotians have affected the legislative process. It is my pleasure to tell the House that Liberals support the speedy passage of Bill C-75.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this particular Bill. It is an area with respect to which I am not particularly well informed. However, there is a principle here which needs to be considered.
I have often wondered why it is that we think that all our non-renewable resources have to be spent as quickly as possible. That idea is the position that has been taken by much of the world's oil industry. It has been taken all over the world and, to a great extent, it has been supported by Governments around the world. In this case, the interest of companies in the Georges Bank and the development of the industry in that area ended up in a rather bitter fight between the oil exploiters and the fishermen of Georges Bank. It is good to know that in this particular situation a good look was taken at the responsibilities and the needs of both groups.
A moratorium is being imposed which gives both groups the opportunity to assure themselves that one will not hurt the other in any way when, sometime in the future, there is the possibility of development of the industry on Georges Bank. There are several attractive features in the plan which are being developed in this particular Bill by the Minister. These are positions which might be models for the future.
July 7, 1988

The previous Liberal Government took a similar type of approach in looking at the Mackenzie Valley as a source of gas and a pipeline which would have traversed all of Canada. It ended up making a recommendation, and following the recommendation which put that particular pipeline on hold. As it happens, the events have caught up to the pipeline. It now seems much less of an economic requirement. This might happen in the case of the Georges Bank as well.
The Bill establishes a model which might be used in the future with respect to the development of other resources and other conflicts that arise between industries. It is refreshing, and 1 must say unusual, to have the will of the people override the desire of large corporations to make more money. That is exactly what this particular Bill is dealing with, the desire of the industry to exploit the gas on Georges Bank, and it is against that group of people who think that perhaps it is not worth doing so. There are other examples of the use of resources to increase the value and the standard of living of part of the population. In some cases, that type of use of resources becomes worth-while. In other cases, development of resources can go in the opposite direction and do more harm to the population than good.
For example, in the development of its North Sea oil, Norway decided that the speed of development should be at the requirement of the country rather than at the requirement of the oil industry. Norway set a timetable which allowed the development to the extent that it did make for a real change in the life structure of Norwegians. Norway used the benefits from those resources to improve the lifestyle of Norwegians without a boom structure. The significance of that type of approach is very important, and it needs to be looked at and perhaps it can become a model for resource development or other industrial development in certain areas.
The previous speaker indicated that not only has it helped in giving opportunities to the fishermen and the people of Nova Scotia to decide on the direction of their lives and the type of lifestyle they want to live, but it served as an example to the United States. I have here a letter from possibly the next President of the United States, Michael Dukakis. He wrote to his Department of the Interior telling them that the Commonwealth of Massachusetts was extremely pleased that Canada was doing what it was doing, and suggesting that the United States take similar action in ensuring that the banks were not disturbed without knowing exactly what the effects would be.
It is refreshing to note that all political Parties here, and the two Parties in Nova Scotia, backed the idea and the Bill. I must express concern on the part of the fishermen that, although they appreciate the 12-year moratorium and the panel being put in place, they have a concern that at some time at the end of the moratorium drilling might start with the support and blessing of both Governments without an investigation into its effect.
We in the New Democratic Party also support the passage of this Bill right now.

My colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan), referred to the fact that it affected some 6,000 fishermen in Nova Scotia. It affects the 6,000 fishermen plus all the fish plant workers who depend on the products of Georges Banks, the lucrative scallops, the groundfish, and the lobsters that are caught in that area. There are hundreds of millions of dollars worth of landed fish values from that area taken on shore every year. Therefore, it affects thousands and thousands of people, for example, fish plant workers, cab drivers, and all the people who are directly and indirectly associated and dependent on the fishery.
It affects a great number of communities that I represent that have depended on the fishery for hundreds of years. In most of those communities fishing is all that they know, communities such as Argyle, Yarmouth, and Digby, and communities that I do not represent on the south shore such as Lunenburg, Shelburne, and Lockeport. On the one hand fishermen and people like myself were approaching the Minister and stating that we do not want this to happen, and on the other hand the oil companies from the West indicated that they wanted to do some drilling on Georges Banks. The Minister had a difficult choice to make. There were no studies available that specifically stated that there should be no drilling. The Minister decided to do what was right. He went to southwestern Nova Scotia and communities such as Pubnico and Yarmouth. He met with the fishermen, and he met with people who depend on the fishery. He walked the streets of Pubnico and Yarmouth and talked to individual citizens and asked: "Should we drill on Georges Bank?" He received a resounding answer.
The point I am attempting to make is that the Minister decided not to listen to the people around him. He spoke to the people of the area. That is what is important. The NDP, the socialist Party, thinks that it has a monopoly on the concerns of people. That is not the case. We are seeing the results of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who was courageous and went against what would normally be called "the flow of things", and what would normally be called "the big company interest". He went with the people. The Minister showed leadership, and I certainly appreciate that leadership.

July 7, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
The Parliamentary Secretary referred to the previous Government's unilateral strategy of imposing a National Energy Program on the people of the West. I wish to remind my colleague, the Hon. July 7, 1988

Because we are dealing with uranium, and I suppose this is true with almost any resource development, there is a real need to develop long-lasting and effective environmental protection structures. There are special problems associated with uranium mining. Control is more easily developed by public corporations than by private corporations. The bottom line is too important to the private corporation which has a tendency to cut as many environmental corners as it can. That is a standard approach which has been a problem in other resource development industries and other manufacturing concerns across the country.

It is not a good Bill for the people of Canada who are taking on the debt of Eldorado and it is not good for the people of Saskatchewan who are taking on the debt of the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too am pleased to speak on the amendment standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) to the Government's legislation, which is to authorize the reorganization and divestiture of Eldorado Nuclear Limited and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof.
The reason we are in favour of a hoist on the proclamation of this legislation is that we believe that the Government has not really studied it. We believe that promises made by the former Minister of Privatization, the new Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall), have not been kept. We believe that the native people of northern Saskatchewan are not adequately protected by this legislation.
I would like to spend most of my time speaking about the pension problem. In a statement earlier today, I pointed out that a promise made by the previous Minister of Privatization was that existing pension plans would be protected and would continue to exist. That promise has been broken by the corporation. In some briefings it gave to employees in the last couple of days, the new corporation has indicated that the status of the surplus in the pension plans will be distributed in such a way that the workers who are currently there will not have the same protection in the future as they have at this time.
The Minister made a direct promise in a press release. It was a direct promise that was again made by the company
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
when it appeared before the standing committee of this House. Even before this legislation was brought back to the House for consideration at report stage, the companies announced that they have a new plan, which means that those people who are already retired will be protected and the surplus will be used to help them, but those workers who remain with Eldorado will not be covered by cost-of-living increases in the future, as would have been the case before the privatization.
I believe that for the sake of honour, the Government which made this promise when it said it wanted to privatize this company should look into what has happened in the last couple of days. As I indicated earlier today, we will not allow this legislation to go to third reading tonight because we want the Government to take this opportunity to investigate what we consider to be very serious charges which we made in the House of Commons earlier today. At 2.15 p.m. today, we made the Government aware of that intention. We believe it would be extremely foolish for this House to pass this Bill at report stage and third reading at this time without investigating this matter.
Time after time, those workers have been told that their present plan would be protected. That issue came before the committee as well. Motion No. 1 standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North would have provided that any surplus in the pension plans of Eldorado and any subsidiary of Eldorado shall be used only for the benefit of current contributors and pensioners and their beneficiaries. We wanted in the legislation the protection that would ensure that that surplus would be used in such a way that those workers, past and present, would be protected.
The Speaker, in his good judgment, said that we could not introduce that motion because it went beyond the scope of the Government's Bill. It may be beyond the scope of the Government's Bill, and it may be technically out of order, but it does not go beyond the scope of the promise the Government made to those workers.
The use of surplus funds in pension plans is a very political issue in Canada. The employees, past and present, believe that they were promised that they would have the same protection now as they had before the effort to privatize Eldorado Nuclear. They believed that they had that assurance from the Minister. She said so in her press release, and she further stated it in a statement she sent to the employees.
This is an issue which deserves investigation. We cannot let this legislation pass until the Government has investigated this matter and assured the workers that that promise made by the Government will be kept.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very serious matter that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) has raised in the House. It is not a matter that is new to the House either.

July 7, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
Several years ago, amendments to the Pension Benefits Standards Act were before the House. In those amendments, there was no mention at all of what would happen to surplus pension funds, more adequately and properly called excess earnings of a pension plan. For that very reason, I moved an amendment to the Pension Benefits Standards Act at that time which would have guaranteed that any excess earnings of pension plans would belong to the pension plans and that no employer had the unilateral right to claim those excess earnings as if they belonged to the employer.
The argument I made at that time, an argument which I think still holds true today, is that a pension plan, like any other benefit that an employee enjoys in an arrangement with an employer, belongs to that employee because it is deferred wages. It is deferred wages in the sense that a group of employees in a bargaining unit enter into negotiations with an employer for a collective agreement and there are certain elements in that collective agreement whereby the employees agree that rather than accept money on a weekly basis in the way of salary increases, they decide with the employer's agreement to defer some of that salary to pay for other benefits such as benefits paid under private pension plans.
That argument is one with which employers generally do not agree because they tend to view these excess earnings as a benefit that comes to them as a matter of right. That is an argument I reject, quite frankly.
Several years ago, one of the largest grabs that was ever made to a pension plan was made by Conrad Black in the Dominion Store employee case. This gave rise to a number of court cases. It was finally concluded about a year ago, I believe, that some if not all of that money did in fact belong to the employees, and Conrad Black was directed to pay those moneys back to the employees. That was done for the very same reasons that I argued here. Those moneys in the pension plan belong to the employee. They are deferred wages that the employee passed up in order to secure a benefit under the pension plan and therefore belong to them.
In this particular case, as I understand it, the employer is doing exactly the same. There are surplus funds in this pension plan and there has been absolutely no discussion and no attempt at negotiating with the union on behalf of the employees as to how those excess earnings should be used. Should they be used to increase benefits under the plan? Should they be used to provide another and different benefit to the employees? Nothing like that has gone on.
1 am sure that in the transition period there will be certain disruptions in the workforce. It would not surprise me at all to find that many members of that workforce with 25, 30 or 36 years of service may find themselves on a scrap heap, so to speak. They deserve better. While I make the key argument that surplus funds in any pension plan belong to the employees,
I would not be adverse to the employer sitting down with the
union and attempting to negotiate the disposition of those surplus funds. However, the option has to be there. The employer has absolutely no right at all to take those funds and use them in any way be wishes.
This is a very serious matter, and I agree with what the Hon. Member for Churchill said. This Party will not agree to third reading of this Bill tonight. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) gave assurances to those employees and their union that those surplus pension funds would be protected, therefore the Minister has some obligation to reassure those employees and the union that those funds will be used on behalf of the employees concerned. That must be done before we agree to third reading. That is the Government's obligation at the very minimum.
In addition, I think it is high time that we took another look at the Pension Benefits Standards Act and amended it to make it illegal for an employee to treat a pension plan in this manner. Both opposition Parties supported my amendment in the House to that effect, and it should have been done two years ago. If it had been, we would not be facing this problem today. Neither would these employees, many of whom have long service with the company and are entitled to much better treatment than they appear to be getting today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak to this amendment calling for a five-year delay in the coming into force of these provisions following proclamation.
As other Members have said, we would prefer that this privatization not take place at all. There are several good reasons for that, apart from the ones which have been spoken to such as pensions and protection of workers. Obviously, with the price of uranium today this is not a favourable time to be selling this company. To do so, the Government effectively has had to write off Eldorado's accumulated debt and excuse the corporation from anything but a very limited responsibility for the environmental clean-up. That is a very important issue and it should be studied and addressed more carefully over the five-year period that we are asking for in the amendment.
The environmental issues surrounding such industries as this one are extremely serious. We have just heard the results of the conferences held on the environment and the consequences of inadequate environmental protection. No longer, as we so clearly know, can one industry assume that the effect it has on the environment will not have important consequences, not only on local areas or a country but globally as well. Therefore, this issue really does require extended study.
Another area that I would particularly like to address is that of benefits to certain targeted groups. One thing that has been done, as a Member outlined previously, was an attempt to ensure that northerners and native people have access to these jobs. While it had not been accomplished totally, it was at least a principle that this Crown corporation was attempting to
July 7, 1988

implement. 1 think it is clear to all of us that a Crown corporation can have somewhat more latitude in this area and should indeed operate not only with the principle of making a profit but also ensuring that the objectives of its policies, both economic and labour, are in the interests of the workers and the country in general. Certainly making a profit is important, but management should have as one of its principles the taking into account of these other factors.
We have the example of other industries. The limestone project in Manitoba is one where local employment has proven to be extremely effective. Local workers have been hired. We have concerns about this in my own riding where we see the impending sale of the Northwest Telephone Corporation. We are attempting to ensure that the 400 NTC jobs which currently exist in Whitehorse will remain. While that number of jobs in a large urban area may not be a serious consideration, certainly in the smaller areas where mines such as that of Eldorado Nuclear are located there is a need to ensure that workers have either the ability to be retrained or they have an opportunity to participate in the workforce.
Certainly this issue was raised by several groups when they appeared before the committee. The steelworkers, for example, raised some particular concerns when they said, "We have learned the hard way to be wary of mergers. In this case we have received half-hearted assurances that there will be no job loss as a result of the merger. Our members deserve more. They deserve an ironclad commitment that there will be no lay-offs as a result of the merger".
The steelworkers' proposal was that the new company employ a minimum number of jobs at each local, making allowances for the fact that obviously uranium mining is a cyclical business. This proposal for a five-year delay in implementation would allow for the kind of adjustment that may be necessary and would take into account the cyclical nature of non-renewable resource development.
It does seem, however, that the major privatizations tend to favour management rather than the interests of workers. Management no longer has to meet the objectives of a Crown corporation or even set an example in health and safety conditions which are particularly important and necessary in an industry such as this one. As I mentioned earlier, over the five-year period there could be much greater study on both health and safety standards for employees and environmental consequences.
In this particular industry and others similar to it there is often very high unemployment. We have already addressed the commitment of the Government of Saskatchewan, which in its focus on developing non-renewable resources in northern Saskatchewan really attempted to develop a model for the integration of aboriginal people and other people living in those more remote areas. As we have seen by that example, it does require a commitment and a plan. The circumstances
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
which led to the Saskatchewan policy were clearly well planned out and well thought out.
The proposed amendment would allow time to deal with these important issues which have long-term consequences for the workers, the environment, and the industry.
